newsitem.title: USA: New England a safe haven for gays and lesbians.
newsitem.headline: New England a safe haven for gays and lesbians.

text.p: New Hampshire Gov. Jeanne Shaheen is expected to sign into a law a gay rights bill later this week making the one-time bulwark of conservatism the 11th state to offer protection against discrimination to lesbians and gay men.

Shaheen's signature will mean gay men and lesbians can find a measure of protection in the areas of employment, housing and accommodation from Lake Champlain east to the Atlantic and from Long Island Sound north to the Canadian border.
Historians were not surprised that New England, a region settled by puritans who burned witches at the stake, has become a sanctuary of sorts for gay men and lesbians.
"The puritan heritage is one of dissent," Middlebury College history professor Holly Allen said, adding "it is intertwined with alternative sexual practices.
"The puritans came to America in order to establish alternative communities...and a frontier society is one where people have come to look for freedom of expression and freedom of lifestyle."
She pointed to New Englander John Humphrey Noyes, founder of the Oneida community in New York during the 19th century who advocated free love and non-monogamous relationships.

"Then there were the Shaker communities throughout the region. They advocated total sexual abstinence...So alternative sexual practices, along with alternative religous practices have long been a part of New England," Allen added.

Tufts University history professor John Brooke said, "New England is the heart of all sorts of reform movements. In the 1830s, it was seen as the bastion of reform movements particularly abolitionism."

Shaheen's signature means that "New Hampshire has finally joined the rest of New England," he said. He credits her election -- she is the first woman to hold the office and the first Democrat in 12 years -- with the changing political climate in the state.
"The usual conservative climate in New Hampshire has been corrupted by the flow of people from Massachusetts into the southern part of the state," he said.

But Amelia Craig, executive director of the Gay and Lesbian Advocates and Defenders, a legal group in New England, noted, "New Hampshire is a conservative state, but also has a libertarian tradition and believes in personal freedom."
Maine Gov. Angus King signed a similar bill May 16 saying, "We have enemies in Maine. They are poverty, disease, ignorance. They are not gay people."

Kevin Cathcart, executive director of Lambda Legal Defense and Education Fund, the nation's largest gay legal group, said the signing of civil rights legislation by both New Hampshire and Maine signal a trend.

"There is the political saying that as Maine goes so the Union and I think in this case that continues to be true. New Hampshire and Maine passing legislation like this so close together I think provides a trend and a boost for the rest of the country.

"For a state like New Hampshire, which does not have a reputation for having a liberal legislature, is an incredibly strong statement for other legislatures," Cathcart added, noting both Iowa and Maryland were considering similar measures.

Barbara Smith, a professor at Radcliff College's Bunting Institute echoed Cathcart's remarks saying, "More and more people today are getting more and more information that lesbians and gays are part of their communities.
"And while it is important to have bills that protect civil rights a lot more needs to be done to be able to live in a society that is a just one."
